meta.what: The ladder below the silicon crystal (atom, inner electrons, nucleus, nucleon, quark, electron, Planck length), a dopant side branch, and the wrap that closes the ladder into a circle (the cosmic uroboros), with an early-universe time track and the stellar origin of the chip's silicon.

meta.honesty: The wrap is a conceptual link, not a physical continuation of space: nothing lies 'past' the observable universe in the sense of the ladder, and the page says so on the wrap level. The physical links it shows are real and sourced: looking out is looking back in time (the CMB, the first nuclei, the quark-gluon plasma), the chip's silicon was made in stars, and inflation (a hypothesis) would make the galaxies' seeds quantum fluctuations.

levels.name: A silicon atom
levels.attach: below lib.si (the silicon crystal's unit cell)
levels.size_note: the distance between neighbouring atoms in the crystal, sqrt(3)/4 x a = 0.2352 nm (a from CODATA 2022); each atom's share is a sphere of radius 117.6 pm. Measured covalent radius 111 pm (Cordero 2008).
levels.blurb: One of the crystal's atoms: a tiny nucleus with 14 electrons around it. Only the outer four take part in bonds and in electronics; the other ten sit deep inside, held 20 to 300 times more tightly.

facts.text: Silicon has 14 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second and 4 in the third (ground configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p2).
facts.source: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, Ground levels and ionization energies, spectra Si I to Si XIV, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl (read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: Removing the outer four electrons one at a time costs 8.15, 16.35, 33.49 and 45.14 eV; the fifth, the first of the inner ten, costs 166.8 eV, and the last (1s) electron 2,673 eV.
facts.source: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, Ground levels and ionization energies, spectra Si I to Si XIV, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl (read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: The four outer (valence) electrons each pair with an electron of a neighbouring atom: four covalent bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, which is what builds the diamond-cubic crystal.
facts.source: S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors)

facts.text: In the crystal neighbouring atoms are 0.235 nm apart, and there are 49.9 atoms in every cubic nanometre (5.0 x 10^22 per cm3).
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: Breaking the crystal into free atoms costs 4.63 eV per atom: about 2.3 eV per bond, since each atom shares four bonds and each bond has two ends.
facts.source: C. Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th ed. (Wiley, 2005), ch. 3, Table 1 (cohesive energies): Si 4.63 eV per atom

facts.text: Natural silicon is 92.22% silicon-28, 4.69% silicon-29 and 3.09% silicon-30; its standard atomic weight is 28.084-28.086.
facts.source: NIST, Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions for Silicon, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/Compositions/stand_alone.pl?ele=Si (read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: Band gap 1.12 eV at 300 K: an electron needs that much energy to leave its bond and move freely. The thermal energy kT at 300 K is 25.85 meV, 43 times smaller.
facts.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Silicon (Si): basic parameters" and "band structure and carrier concentration" (www.ioffe.ru/SVA/NSM/Semicond/Si/), compiled from Sze, Shur and others; NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)
facts.note: kT derived from the Boltzmann constant (exact)

facts.text: So pure silicon at room temperature has only about 10^10 free electrons per cm3: one for every 5 x 10^12 atoms.
facts.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Silicon (Si): basic parameters" and "band structure and carrier concentration" (www.ioffe.ru/SVA/NSM/Semicond/Si/), compiled from Sze, Shur and others; NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: A FinFET channel of about 6 x 16.5 x 52 nm holds about 257,000 silicon atoms and, on average, 5 x 10^-8 thermally freed electrons: none. The transistor conducts only when the gate voltage pulls electrons in from the heavily doped source.
facts.source: the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si); Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Silicon (Si): basic parameters" and "band structure and carrier concentration" (www.ioffe.ru/SVA/NSM/Semicond/Si/), compiled from Sze, Shur and others
facts.note: the channel's size is the chip page's inference (TSMC does not publish N7's); the conduction picture is the textbook MOSFET (Sze ch. 6)

facts.text: With more than 24 billion transistors and about 257,000 atoms per fin's channel, the chip's channels hold at least 6 x 10^15 silicon atoms: about 0.3 micrograms if each transistor has one fin, about a microgram if three. That is all the silicon that actually switches.
facts.source: the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si); docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/facts.json (chip.process): TSMC 7 nm, more than 24 billion transistors (Esperanto, Hot Chips 33 and IEEE Micro 2022)
facts.note: the transistor count is Esperanto's; fins per transistor and N7's channel size are not published, so this is an order of magnitude

facts.text: Its share of the crystal (a sphere of radius 118 pm) is about 32,000 times wider than its nucleus.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 3: R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm

levels.draw: Drawn SVG: the atom at the centre with its four bonds to the neighbours' edges (tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees, drawn in projection); a soft cloud for the four valence electrons; a small bright core labelled "10 inner electrons and the nucleus"; a scale bar of 0.1 nm. Reuses lib.si's ball-and-stick style.
levels.zoom_note: the jump from p.core to p.nucleus is the long empty one (about 1,000x) and from p.quark to p.planck the longest (about 10^16x); like the outside ladder's long steps, they should be 'jump' moves with a drawn factor much smaller than the true one.

levels.name: A dopant atom (phosphorus or boron)
levels.attach: a sibling of p.atom: an atom of the source or drain (lib.sd if the ladder adds it) or, rarely, of the channel
levels.size_note: a substituted atom takes a silicon atom's place in the lattice; covalent radii P 107 pm, B 84 pm, As 119 pm, Ge 120 pm, Si 111 pm (Cordero 2008)
levels.blurb: A foreign atom in a silicon atom's place. Phosphorus brings five outer electrons, one more than the bonds need, and that spare electron is free to carry current; boron brings three, leaving a gap (a hole) that carries current the other way. This is how a transistor's source and drain are made to conduct.

facts.text: Phosphorus and arsenic are donors in silicon: the spare electron is held by only 0.045 eV (P) or 0.054 eV (As). Boron is an acceptor, at 0.045 eV.
facts.source: Ioffe Institute, NSM Archive, "Silicon (Si): basic parameters" and "band structure and carrier concentration" (www.ioffe.ru/SVA/NSM/Semicond/Si/), compiled from Sze, Shur and others

facts.text: Those energies are only about 2 kT at room temperature (2 kT = 52 meV), so nearly every dopant atom has given up (or taken) its electron.
facts.source: S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors); NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: In a TSMC FinFET patent, the n-type source/drain is epitaxial silicon or silicon carbide with phosphorus (Si:P, SiCP), which pulls the channel under tension; the p-type source/drain is silicon-germanium (10-40% germanium in the first layer, 20-80% in the second) doped with boron (5 x 10^20 to 10^22 per cm3 in the second layer), which squeezes the channel.
facts.source: TSMC, US Patent 11,107,923 B2, "Source/drain regions of FinFET devices and methods of forming same" (priority 14 Jun 2019), description (a patent's embodiments, not a statement about N7)
facts.note: a patent's embodiments; TSMC does not say which apply to N7. Tension speeds electrons and compression speeds holes.

facts.text: TSMC's IEDM 2016 7 nm paper describes epitaxially raised sources and drains that strain the channel, and a contact structure designed to reduce resistance.
facts.source: C. Edwards, "7nm finFET process techniques lead IEDM lineup", Tech Design Forums, 24 Oct 2016 (on S.-Y. Wu et al., TSMC, IEDM 2016 paper 2.6)

facts.text: 10^21 dopant atoms per cm3 is one per cubic nanometre, among 50 silicon atoms: about 1 atom in 50. At 10^22, one in 5.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: So much doping is needed at the contacts: a metal on lightly doped silicon forms a barrier (a Schottky barrier); heavy doping makes it thin enough for electrons to tunnel through. For 7 nm-class technology a contact resistivity below 2 x 10^-9 ohm cm2 is the stated goal.
facts.source: IBM, US Patent 10,431,502 B1, "Maskless epitaxial growth of phosphorus-doped Si and boron-doped SiGe (Ge) for advanced source/drain contact" (priority 16 Apr 2018), background; S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors)

facts.text: The same patent dopes the wells under the fins at 10^16 to 10^18 per cm3. At those levels a 6 x 16.5 x 52 nm channel would hold on average 0.05 to 5.1 dopant atoms, among some 257,000 silicon atoms: a handful at most, and their random number and place would make every transistor different. FinFET channels are therefore left nearly undoped and the threshold voltage is set by the gate metal instead.
facts.source: TSMC, US Patent 11,107,923 B2, "Source/drain regions of FinFET devices and methods of forming same" (priority 14 Jun 2019), description (a patent's embodiments, not a statement about N7); the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si); S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors)
facts.note: whether N7 dopes its channels, and how much, is not published (unknown); the count is arithmetic on an inferred volume and the patent's well range

levels.draw: Drawn SVG: the crystal view of p.atom with one atom recoloured (P or B, toggle), its spare electron (or hole) drawn as a large faint orbit several atoms wide; caption "1 atom in 50 in the source and drain; maybe none in the channel".

levels.name: The inner electrons
levels.attach: between p.atom and p.nucleus (a bridging level, like the outside ladder's optional levels)
levels.size_note: twice the most probable radius of a 2p electron in a hydrogen-like model with Clementi's effective charge 9.945: 4 a0 / 9.945 = 21.3 pm; the two 1s electrons peak at a0 / 13.575 = 3.9 pm
levels.blurb: Ten electrons fill the first two shells, packed close around the nucleus. They are held so tightly that chemistry and electronics never move them; they only screen most of the nucleus's charge from the outer four.

facts.text: The 1s pair sits about 3.9 pm from the nucleus and the 2s and 2p eight about 21 pm: the outer four, around 118 pm, are some 5 to 30 times farther out.
facts.source: E. Clementi and D. L. Raimondi, "Atomic screening constants from SCF functions", J. Chem. Phys. 38, 2686 (1963): Si Zeff 1s 13.575, 2p 9.945 (as tabulated in Wikipedia, "Effective nuclear charge"); NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)
facts.note: hydrogen-like estimate with effective nuclear charges; good for the nodeless 1s and 2p orbitals

facts.text: The 1s electrons feel almost the full nuclear charge (an effective 13.6 of 14); the 3p electrons feel only 4.3, because the inner ten stand in between.
facts.source: E. Clementi and D. L. Raimondi, "Atomic screening constants from SCF functions", J. Chem. Phys. 38, 2686 (1963): Si Zeff 1s 13.575, 2p 9.945 (as tabulated in Wikipedia, "Effective nuclear charge")

facts.text: The innermost electron of a silicon atom is bound by 2,673 eV, more than 300 times an outer electron's 8.15 eV.
facts.source: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, Ground levels and ionization energies, spectra Si I to Si XIV, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl (read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: An electron in an atom is not a little ball on an orbit: the shells are clouds of probability, and the radii here are where each cloud is densest.
facts.source: S. M. Sze and K. K. Ng, Physics of Semiconductor Devices, 3rd ed. (Wiley, 2007), ch. 1 (crystal, bands, donors and acceptors)

levels.draw: Drawn SVG: radial-density rings (1s small and bright, 2s/2p a ring at about 21 pm), the valence cloud as a faint rim at the frame's edge; a scale bar of 10 pm.

levels.name: The silicon-28 nucleus
levels.size_note: diameter from R = 1.2 fm x 28^(1/3) = 3.64 fm (Krane); the measured rms charge radius is 3.1224 fm, which a uniform sphere of radius 4.03 fm would have. A nucleus has a soft edge, so any radius is a convention.
levels.blurb: Fourteen protons and fourteen neutrons, packed together by the strong force: a thirty-thousandth of the atom's width but 99.97% of its mass. Nothing in a chip ever touches it.

facts.text: Silicon-28: 14 protons and 14 neutrons, stable.
facts.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021))

facts.text: Nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm: for A = 28, R = 3.64 fm, about 7.3 fm across.
facts.source: K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 3: R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm

facts.text: Measured rms charge radius 3.1224 +/- 0.0024 fm.
facts.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021))

facts.text: The nucleus holds 99.97% of the atom's mass; the 14 electrons, 0.027%.
facts.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021)); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf)

facts.text: Its density is about 2.3 x 10^17 kg per m3: a teaspoon (5 mL) of nuclear matter would weigh about 1.1 billion tonnes.
facts.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021)); K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 3: R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm

facts.text: If the nucleus were a 1 cm marble, the atom's share of the crystal would be about 320 m across: an atom is almost all empty space.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 3: R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm

facts.text: Binding energy 8.448 MeV per nucleon, 237 MeV in all: the nucleus weighs 0.9% less than its 28 separate parts (E = mc^2).
facts.source: IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021))

facts.text: That is about a million times the energy of the outer electrons (8.15 eV) or of a chemical bond (about 2.3 eV): why chemistry, and electronics, never change a nucleus.

C 45, 030003 (2021)); NIST Atomic Spectra Database, Ground levels and ionization energies, spectra Si I to Si XIV, physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl (read 1 Oct 2026); C. Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics, 8th ed. (Wiley, 2005), ch. 3, Table 1 (cohesive energies): Si 4.63 eV per atom

levels.draw: Drawn SVG: a cluster of 28 overlapping spheres (14 proton-coloured, 14 neutron-coloured) with a soft edge; scale bar 1 fm; a small inset showing the atom with the nucleus as an invisible dot ("this is 1/32,000 of the atom").

levels.name: A proton (and its twin, the neutron)
levels.attach: one of the 28 nucleons in p.nucleus
levels.size_note: twice the proton's rms charge radius, 0.84075(64) fm (CODATA 2022; PDG 2026)
levels.blurb: A proton is three quarks (up, up, down) held by gluons; a neutron is up, down, down. Unlike the electron, it has a real size, because it is a bound state, and most of its mass is the energy of what goes on inside.

facts.text: Proton rms charge radius 0.84075 +/- 0.00064 fm.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

facts.text: Older electron-scattering measurements gave about 0.88 fm; muonic-hydrogen spectroscopy gave 0.84 fm, the 'proton radius puzzle'. The Particle Data Group still notes that the two kinds of measurement are not averaged.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

facts.text: Proton mass 938.272 MeV/c^2, neutron 939.565 MeV/c^2: each about 1836 times an electron's.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

facts.text: Quark content: proton uud, neutron udd. Charges +2/3 e for up and -1/3 e for down give +1 and 0.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: quarks (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-quarks.pdf)

facts.text: A free neutron decays in 878.3 +/- 0.4 s on average; bound in silicon-28 it is stable.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf); IAEA Nuclear Data Section, LiveChart of Nuclides data service, 28Si ground state (nds.iaea.org/relnsd/v1/data?fields=ground_states&nuclides=28si, read 1 Oct 2026): charge radius from I. Angeli and K. P. Marinova, At. Data Nucl. Data Tables 99, 69 (2013); mass and binding energy from AME2020 (M. Wang et al., Chinese Phys. C 45, 030003 (2021))

facts.text: The neutron has no charge, but its charge is spread unevenly: its mean-square charge radius is negative (-0.1155 fm^2), meaning a positive core and a negative outer part.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

facts.text: No proton has ever been seen to decay: its lifetime exceeds 2.4 x 10^34 years for the decay to a positron and a pion (the universe is 1.4 x 10^10 years old).
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf); Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1

facts.text: Each silicon-28 atom holds 42 up and 42 down quarks (84 in all); a 6 x 16.5 x 52 nm channel's ~257,000 atoms hold some 22 million quarks and 3.6 million electrons.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf); the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si)
facts.note: the per-atom count is arithmetic (derived); the channel count rests on the inferred channel size

levels.draw: Drawn SVG: a soft sphere 1.68 fm across with three coloured dots (red, green, blue: colour charge, not real colours) joined by wavy gluon lines, and faint quark-antiquark pairs; caption "the dots are drawn far too big: a quark is less than 1/2000 of this".

levels.name: A quark
levels.attach: one of the three quarks drawn in p.nucleon
levels.size_note: no size has ever been measured: the 95% upper limit on a quark's effective radius is 0.43 x 10^-16 cm = 4.3 x 10^-19 m (ZEUS 2016). The frame shows the limit, not the quark.
levels.blurb: As far as any experiment can tell, a quark is a point. The disc here is only the limit: if a quark has a size, it is smaller than this, under a two-thousandth of the proton. Quarks are never found alone; pull one out and the energy makes new quarks.

facts.text: Upper limit on the effective quark radius: 4.3 x 10^-19 m (95% confidence), from electron-proton collisions at HERA.
facts.source: ZEUS Collaboration, "Limits on the effective quark radius from inclusive ep scattering at HERA", Phys. Lett. B 757, 468 (2016), arXiv:1604.01280

facts.text: The proton is at least 1,955 times wider than a quark could be.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); ZEUS Collaboration, "Limits on the effective quark radius from inclusive ep scattering at HERA", Phys. Lett. B 757, 468 (2016), arXiv:1604.01280

facts.text: Masses (MS-bar at 2 GeV): up 2.16 +/- 0.07 MeV, down 4.70 +/- 0.07 MeV. Two ups and a down add to 9.0 MeV: 1% of the proton's 938.3 MeV.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: quarks (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-quarks.pdf); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)
facts.note: quark masses depend on the scheme and scale they are quoted at; the simple sum is an illustration

facts.text: A lattice-QCD breakdown of the proton's mass: the quarks' masses (through the quark condensate, u, d and s) give 9%, the quarks' energy of motion 33%, the gluon field's energy 37%, and the 'trace anomaly' 23%.
facts.source: Y.-B. Yang et al. (chiQCD), "Proton mass decomposition from the QCD energy momentum tensor", Phys. Rev. Lett. 121, 212001 (2018), arXiv:1808.08677

facts.text: Lattice QCD computes the proton's and neutron's masses from the quark and gluon theory, matching experiment.
facts.source: S. Duerr et al., "Ab initio determination of light hadron masses", Science 322, 1224 (2008), arXiv:0906.3599

facts.text: Gluons carry the strong force between quarks; they are massless in theory (a mass of a few MeV is not excluded) and come in eight colour states.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: gauge and Higgs bosons, gluon (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-gauge-higgs-bosons.pdf); Particle Data Group (2026), review 15, Quark Model (C. Amsler, V. Crede et al., rev. Aug 2025), sec. 15.1-15.2

facts.text: Colour is believed to be permanently confined: only colourless combinations (three quarks, or a quark and an antiquark) exist on their own.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 15, Quark Model (C. Amsler, V. Crede et al., rev. Aug 2025), sec. 15.1-15.2

facts.text: Squeezing quarks into 0.84 fm gives them energies around hbar c / r = 235 MeV each: why most of a proton's mass is energy rather than quark mass.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)
facts.note: an uncertainty-principle estimate, order of magnitude only

levels.draw: Drawn SVG: a dashed circle labelled "limit: 4.3 x 10^-19 m" with a point at the centre that never grows; a scale bar of 10^-19 m; a side note "no experiment has found any size". Same treatment for p.electron.

levels.name: An electron
levels.attach: one of the 14 electrons of p.atom (a side branch: double-click an electron cloud)
levels.size_note: no size has ever been measured: a search for contact interactions at the LEP collider puts any radius below 2 x 10^-20 m (as quoted by the Gabrielse group). The frame shows the limit.
levels.blurb: The particle that carries every current in the chip. Its charge and mass are known to 10 digits, but no experiment has found any size: as far as we know it is a point. The 'cloud' of the atom is where the electron is likely to be, not the electron itself.

facts.text: Charge -1.602176634 x 10^-19 C, exactly (it defines the coulomb since 2019); mass 9.1094 x 10^-31 kg = 0.51100 MeV/c^2.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: A radius limit below 2 x 10^-20 m, from contact-interaction searches at LEP at the 10 TeV scale.
facts.source: G. Gabrielse group (Northwestern Center for Fundamental Physics), "Limit on Electron Substructure", cfp.physics.northwestern.edu/gabrielse-group/electron-substructure.html, citing D. Bourilkov, Phys. Rev. D 64, 071701(R) (2001) for the LEP contact-interaction limit

facts.text: Its magnetic moment is measured to about 1 part in 10^13 ((g-2)/2 = 0.00115965218062(12)) and agrees with the theory of a point particle; an electron made of smaller parts would spoil that agreement.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf); G. Gabrielse group (Northwestern Center for Fundamental Physics), "Limit on Electron Substructure", cfp.physics.northwestern.edu/gabrielse-group/electron-substructure.html, citing D. Bourilkov, Phys. Rev. D 64, 071701(R) (2001) for the LEP contact-interaction limit

facts.text: The electron is round: its electric dipole moment is below 4.1 x 10^-30 e cm (PDG 2026), so its charge sits within 4.1 x 10^-32 m of its centre (dipole moment divided by its charge).
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf)

facts.text: The 'classical electron radius', 2.818 fm, is a length built from its charge and mass, not its size.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: Stable: its lifetime exceeds 6.6 x 10^28 years.
facts.source: Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf)

facts.text: Every coulomb that flows through the chip is 6.24 x 10^18 electrons.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

levels.draw: As p.quark: a dashed circle labelled "limit: 2 x 10^-20 m" around a point; scale bar 10^-20 m.

levels.name: The Planck length
levels.attach: the floor of the ladder, below p.quark and p.electron
levels.size_note: Planck length sqrt(hbar G / c^3) = 1.616255(18) x 10^-35 m (CODATA 2022)
levels.blurb: The length built from gravity, quantum mechanics and the speed of light. Here, physicists expect space and time themselves to need a quantum description that nobody has yet; whether anything can be smaller is unknown. Between the quark's limit and here lie 16 powers of ten that no experiment has reached.

facts.text: Planck length 1.616255 x 10^-35 m; Planck time 5.391247 x 10^-44 s.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: Max Planck introduced these natural units of length, mass, time and temperature in 1899.
facts.source: M. Planck, "Ueber irreversible Strahlungsvorgaenge", Sitzungsberichte der Koeniglich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin (1899), pp. 440-480 (natural units of length, mass, time and temperature)

facts.text: The quark's radius limit is 3 x 10^16 times the Planck length: some 16 powers of ten that no experiment has probed.
facts.source: ZEUS Collaboration, "Limits on the effective quark radius from inclusive ep scattering at HERA", Phys. Lett. B 757, 468 (2016), arXiv:1604.01280; NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: Whether the Planck length is a smallest possible length is an open question: thought experiments and several approaches to quantum gravity suggest a minimal length, and none is confirmed.
facts.source: S. Hossenfelder, "Minimal length scale scenarios for quantum gravity", Living Rev. Relativ. 16, 2 (2013), arXiv:1203.6191

facts.text: From the Planck length to the observable universe's diameter is 61.7 powers of ten.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)

levels.draw: Drawn SVG, marked "theory": a foam-like texture fading in (labelled "spacetime here may not be smooth; no one knows"), no particles; a scale bar of 10^-35 m. The readout's mantissa shows 1.6 x 10^-35 m.

levels.name: The cosmic uroboros (a conceptual link)
levels.attach: above beyond (the outermost level) and below p.planck: the join that closes the ladder into a circle
levels.size_note: Not a size. This step is a picture of all the scales at once, not a place: zooming out past the observable universe does not lead to anything physical, and the circle is an idea, not a continuation of space.
levels.blurb: A serpent swallowing its tail: the physicist Sheldon Glashow's picture of all the sizes in nature, from the Planck length at the tail to the observable universe at the head. The circle is a way of seeing, not a place: the largest and smallest scales are joined by physics, not by distance. Looking far out is looking back in time, to an early universe that was a sea of quarks.
levels.honesty: The page must say on this level, in words: "This is not further out in space. The ring is a picture; the links across it are physics." The readout shows "conceptual link" instead of a size, and the move animates along the ring, not as a zoom.

facts.text: Joel Primack and Nancy Ellen Abrams, adapting an idea of Sheldon Glashow (Nobel 1979), drew the 'Cosmic Uroboros': the tip of the tail is the Planck length, the head is the cosmic horizon, about 60 powers of ten apart.
facts.source: J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf); S. L. Glashow's cosmic uroboros, as credited by Primack and Abrams (ch. 6, note 4): first version reproduced in T. Ferris, New York Times Magazine, 26 Sep 1982, p. 38; see also S. L. Glashow with B. Bova, Interactions (Warner Books, 1988), ch. 14 (not read directly)

facts.text: Their first meaning: gravity, negligible from bacteria to atoms, becomes strong again at the tail's tip, so it may link the largest and smallest sizes (a hope of quantum gravity and string theory, not yet tested).
facts.source: J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf)

facts.text: Their second meaning: at the very beginning of the Big Bang the largest scale, the horizon, was not much larger than the smallest; the serpent's body filled in as the universe expanded.
facts.source: J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf)
facts.note: the horizon's growth from near-Planck size rests on extrapolating known physics back to the Planck time

facts.text: Looking out is looking back: the farthest light we can see, the cosmic microwave background, left 380,000 years after the Big Bang; before that the universe was hot, dense and opaque.
facts.source: NASA Science, Physics of the Cosmos, "Big Bang and the Evolution of the Universe", science.nasa.gov/astrophysics/programs/physics-of-the-cosmos/big-bang-and-the-evolution-of-the-universe/ (read 1 Oct 2026); NASA Science, "Cosmic History", science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/ (read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: The early universe is 'the poor man's accelerator' (Zel'dovich): its first minutes reached energies that test particle physics.
facts.source: G. Leconte-Chevillard, "'The poor man's accelerator', or how the primordial universe became a testing ground for particle physics", Synthese 207 (2026), doi:10.1007/s11229-026-05476-2

facts.text: Example: the helium made in the first three minutes limited how many kinds of neutrino could exist (Steigman, Schramm and Gunn, 1977); collider measurements of the Z boson later counted 2.996 +/- 0.007.
facts.source: G. Steigman, D. N. Schramm, J. E. Gunn, "Cosmological limits to the number of massive leptons", Phys. Lett. B 66, 202 (1977); G. Leconte-Chevillard, "'The poor man's accelerator', or how the primordial universe became a testing ground for particle physics", Synthese 207 (2026), doi:10.1007/s11229-026-05476-2; Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: leptons (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-leptons.pdf)

facts.text: On a logarithmic scale the middle of the whole ladder, between the Planck length and the observable universe, is 0.12 mm: about the size of a minion's 4 KB L1 data cache or one SRAM panel of the shire cache in this chip.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond); the chip diagram's own tree (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/inside.json: lib.channel, lib.si)
facts.note: the two chip sizes are the chip page's order-of-magnitude inferences

facts.text: Primack and Abrams place human size near the centre of the uroboros, with their round numbers (10^-33 cm to 10^28 cm).
facts.source: J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf)

levels.draw: Drawn SVG, marked "a picture, not a place": a ring (the serpent) with the page's own levels as ticks around it at log-scale positions (Planck, quark, proton, nucleus, atom, fin, FinFET, cell, minion, shire, die, card, rack, Studio 45, San Francisco, Earth, Sun, Milky Way, Laniakea, observable universe), the head (universe) touching the tail (Planck). Three labelled chords across the ring: "looking out = looking back in time" (universe to quarks), "the chip's atoms were made in stars" (Milky Way to atom), "gravity at both ends?" (dashed: hypothesis). Our own drawing, not a copy of Glashow's or Primack's artwork.

facts.text: Last scattering at redshift z* = 1089.92 +/- 0.25, age 372.6 +/- 1.0 thousand years (Planck 2018 base model).
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; Planck Collaboration, "Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters", A&A 641, A6 (2020)

facts.text: Then the universe was 1 + z* = 1091 times hotter than the CMB's 2.7255 K today: 2,973 K, cool enough for electrons and nuclei to form atoms.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; D. J. Fixsen, "The temperature of the cosmic microwave background", ApJ 707, 916 (2009); NASA Science, "Cosmic History", science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/ (read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: The region that is now our observable universe was then 85 million light-years across.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)
facts.note: today's comoving diameter divided by 1 + z*

facts.text: Its temperature varied by about 1 part in 100,000 from place to place (COBE): the seeds that grew into galaxies.
facts.source: NASA Science, "COBE's Top Discoveries", science.nasa.gov/mission/cobe/science/ (read 1 Oct 2026); NASA Science, "Cosmic History", science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/ (read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: That light is still all around: about 411 CMB photons in every cubic centimetre of space, at 2.7255 K.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; D. J. Fixsen, "The temperature of the cosmic microwave background", ApJ 707, 916 (2009)

facts.text: In the leading theory, inflation, those seeds began as quantum fluctuations on sub-atomic scales, stretched to the size of galaxies: the smallest scales shaping the largest. Planck's measurements fit simple inflation models; inflation is not proven.
facts.source: Planck Collaboration, "Planck 2018 results. X. Constraints on inflation", A&A 641, A10 (2020), arXiv:1807.06211

epochs.name: The first nuclei: about three minutes

facts.text: Deuterium, helium-3, helium-4 and lithium-7 were made at the end of the first three minutes, once the temperature fell to about 0.1 MeV (1.2 billion K); nuclear reactions were fixed by about 180 s.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 24, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (B. D. Fields, P. Molaro, S. Sarkar, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 24.1-24.2

facts.text: Primordial helium is 24.5% of the ordinary matter by mass (Yp = 0.2448 +/- 0.0033). No silicon was made: nuclei heavier than lithium do not form in significant amounts.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; Particle Data Group (2026), review 24, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (B. D. Fields, P. Molaro, S. Sarkar, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 24.1-24.2

facts.text: The region that is now our observable universe was then about 200 light-years across.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)
facts.note: entropy conservation, a T g*s^(1/3) constant, with g*s = 3.91 after electron-positron annihilation

facts.text: There are about 1.66 billion CMB photons for every proton or neutron (eta = 6.04 x 10^-10).
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 2, Astrophysical Constants and Parameters (D. E. Groom, D. Scott, rev. Aug 2025), Table 2.1; Particle Data Group (2026), review 24, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (B. D. Fields, P. Molaro, S. Sarkar, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 24.1-24.2

facts.text: The universe holds matter and almost no antimatter: in the standard reading, matter outnumbered antimatter by a tiny margin early on, and the leftover makes every proton and neutron, including the chip's.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); Particle Data Group (2026), review 24, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (B. D. Fields, P. Molaro, S. Sarkar, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 24.1-24.2

facts.text: Why there was a margin at all (baryogenesis) is unknown: it needs baryon-number violation, C and CP violation and a departure from equilibrium, and several mechanisms are viable.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis)

facts.text: Above about 156.5 MeV (1.8 x 10^12 K) quarks and gluons are not bound into protons and neutrons: a quark-gluon plasma. Lattice QCD puts the crossover at 156.5 +/- 1.5 MeV.
facts.source: A. Bazavov et al. (HotQCD), "Chiral crossover in QCD at zero and non-zero chemical potentials", Phys. Lett. B 795, 15 (2019), arXiv:1812.08235; Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis)

facts.text: The universe cooled through it 14-24 microseconds after the Big Bang.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); A. Bazavov et al. (HotQCD), "Chiral crossover in QCD at zero and non-zero chemical potentials", Phys. Lett. B 795, 15 (2019), arXiv:1812.08235
facts.note: PDG eq. 22.44 with N = 51.25 just above and 17.25 just below the transition

facts.text: The region that is now our observable universe was then about 3,700 to 5,300 times the Earth-Sun distance across (under a tenth of a light-year).
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)

facts.text: At that temperature a typical particle's wavelength, hbar c / kT = 1.26 fm, is the size of a proton: the universe's 'microscope' and the proton's size meet.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026); A. Bazavov et al. (HotQCD), "Chiral crossover in QCD at zero and non-zero chemical potentials", Phys. Lett. B 795, 15 (2019), arXiv:1812.08235; Particle Data Group, F. Takahashi et al., Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 41, 2630011 (2026), summary table: N baryons (p, n) (pdg.lbl.gov/2026/tables/rpp2026-sum-baryons.pdf)

facts.text: The protons and neutrons in the chip's nuclei first formed in this transition; billions of years later, stars built them into silicon.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); J. A. Johnson, "Populating the periodic table: Nucleosynthesis of the elements", Science 363, 474 (2019)

facts.text: The LHC recreates this plasma by colliding lead nuclei, at temperatures more than 100,000 times the centre of the Sun.
facts.source: CERN press release, "Quark Matter 2017: understanding the early universe", 9 Feb 2017, home.cern

epochs.name: Particles get their masses: about 10 picoseconds

facts.text: The Standard Model's electroweak crossover, when the Higgs field takes its value, is at 159.5 +/- 1.5 GeV (lattice).
facts.source: M. D'Onofrio and K. Rummukainen, "Standard model cross-over on the lattice", Phys. Rev. D 93, 025003 (2016), arXiv:1508.07161

facts.text: That was about 9 picoseconds after the Big Bang, when the region that is now our observable universe was about 3 times the Earth-Sun distance across.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); M. D'Onofrio and K. Rummukainen, "Standard model cross-over on the lattice", Phys. Rev. D 93, 025003 (2016), arXiv:1508.07161; the chip diagram's outside ladder (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/outside.json: universe, beyond)
facts.note: PDG eq. 22.44 with all Standard Model particles, N = 106.75

facts.text: In the Standard Model the electron and the quarks get their masses from the Higgs field. The electron's mass sets the size of every atom (the Bohr radius is inversely proportional to it), and so the size of the chip's transistors.
facts.source: Particle Data Group (2026), review 22, Big-Bang Cosmology (K. A. Olive, J. A. Peacock, rev. Aug 2025), sec. 22.3.2 (eq. 22.44, table of N(T)) and 22.3.6 (baryogenesis); NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: Planck time 5.391247 x 10^-44 s: before it, known physics cannot describe the universe.
facts.source: NIST, 2022 CODATA recommended values of the fundamental physical constants, physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants (each constant's values page, read 1 Oct 2026)

facts.text: What happened at or before the Planck time, and whether 'before' means anything, is unknown.
facts.source: S. Hossenfelder, "Minimal length scale scenarios for quantum gravity", Living Rev. Relativ. 16, 2 (2013), arXiv:1203.6191

stardust.name: The chip's silicon was made in stars

facts.text: Silicon is made in massive stars, by oxygen burning late in their lives, and spread by their supernova explosions; exploding white dwarfs make some too.
facts.source: J. A. Johnson, "Populating the periodic table: Nucleosynthesis of the elements", Science 363, 474 (2019); S. E. Woosley, A. Heger, T. A. Weaver, "The evolution and explosion of massive stars", Rev. Mod. Phys. 74, 1015 (2002)

facts.text: The Sun and its planets formed from gas already enriched by earlier stars; the oldest solids in the Solar System are 4,567.30 +/- 0.16 million years old.
facts.source: J. N. Connelly et al., "The absolute chronology and thermal processing of solids in the solar protoplanetary disk", Science 338, 651 (2012); J. R. Primack and N. E. Abrams, The View from the Center of the Universe (Riverhead, 2006), ch. 6, "What Size is the Universe? The Cosmic Uroboros" (chapter text: ncatlab.org/nlab/files/PrimackSizeOfUniverse.pdf)

facts.text: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, more than 25% by weight.
facts.source: L. A. Corathers (USGS), "Mineral resource of the month: silicon", Geotimes (2003), usgs.gov/publications/mineral-resource-month-silicon

facts.text: So the silicon atoms in the chip's fins were forged in stars of the Milky Way more than 4.6 billion years ago, from protons and neutrons formed in the first 20 microseconds: a physical link between the ladder's top and bottom.
facts.source: J. A. Johnson, "Populating the periodic table: Nucleosynthesis of the elements", Science 363, 474 (2019); J. N. Connelly et al., "The absolute chronology and thermal processing of solids in the solar protoplanetary disk", Science 338, 651 (2012); A. Bazavov et al. (HotQCD), "Chiral crossover in QCD at zero and non-zero chemical potentials", Phys. Lett. B 795, 15 (2019), arXiv:1812.08235

constants.source: CODATA 2022 (NIST), Ioffe NSM archive; Si_bond and atoms per nm3 derived

loop.note: Proposed links that close the ladder into a circle. 'up' is the Up button (zoom out), 'in' the default double-click (zoom in). Existing ids are from inside.json and outside.json.
up: shire.panel.array (an L2/L3 SRAM panel of shire 0)
vpu.lane.fma.tree (the compressor tree of minion 0's FMA, lane 0)
loop.exits: On the way back up from the wrap, lib.finfet's Up goes to a memory cell or a compute cell: the page can alternate per turn of the circle, or follow whichever the viewer came down through, defaulting to the memory cell. The wrap level can offer both as buttons ('into a memory cell', 'into a compute transistor').
loop.readout: From beyond to p.planck the readout leaves sizes: it shows 'conceptual link' on p.wrap, and the epochs (if shown) give time and temperature, not size. From p.planck up to p.quark the readout runs through 16 powers of ten marked 'unexplored'.
loop.optional_time_track: e.cmb, e.bbn, e.qcd, e.ew, e.planck can be drawn as a strip on p.wrap (looking out = looking back), or as steps between beyond and p.planck; they are times, not sizes.
